label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
To: timeline
Replying to: none

Subject: none

Spent the last two Saturdays redoing the electric in a buddy's shed and I have not stopped thinking about it, so you're all getting the list. He's staying anonymous. He's got relatives who read Facebook.

Power to the shed was three orange extension cords plugged into each other, out a basement window, across the yard, and under the deck. Under the deck, where nobody ever looks and everything lives.

One of the connections was wrapped in tape. Not electrical tape. DUCT tape. I held it up like a fish I caught.

The shed outlet was wired with speaker wire. Speaker wire. I guess if you're gonna plug in a radio you may as well use the radio part.

The GFCI outlet was a regular outlet with a GFCI sticker on it. That's it. A sticker. Let me be clear that the sticker does not trip.

The ceiling fan box was held up by one drywall screw. One. That fan was a good sneeze away from becoming a floor fan.

There was a mouse nest in a junction box. In fairness to the mice, they were fine. Warm, powered, unbothered. Best housing situation in the neighborhood.

Then the panel. I open the door and written on the inside in Sharpie it says SHED - DONT TOUCH - RON. My buddy's wife is standing right there and goes "who's Ron?" like I'd know. I don't know, Ron. I'll never know Ron. But Ron had a Sharpie and a lot of confidence.

Now the one that actually got me. The breaker feeding all this was a 30 amp. The wire it was feeding was 14 gauge. 14 gauge is good for 15 amps. The breaker is the only thing standing between that wire and a fire, and it was sized so the wire would be glowing inside the wall long before it ever tripped. Nobody does anything wrong that night. Everybody's asleep. That's how it goes.

Here's the thing I'll say for whoever did it. I don't think he was a bad guy. Cheap and a little proud, which is most of these jobs. Nobody sets out to burn a place down. They save a couple hundred bucks, they feel pretty good about it, and the wire doesn't care how they feel.

What I did to fix it: trenched 18 inches down, ran 12/2 UF, put in a 20 amp GFCI breaker, a real box, real outlets, and hung the fan on a proper brace. Payment was two pizzas and a case of Yuengling, which is the correct rate for a buddy and I'd do it again.

I've been doing this 26 years and I can tell you the stuff that scares me is never the big scary-looking stuff. It's the job that works. The lights come on, the fan spins, everybody's happy, and the whole thing is quietly one bad night from a fire truck. Works and safe are two different words.

So please, if you need electrical work done, call a licensed electrician. Get a permit pulled and get it inspected. It costs more than a guy who watched a few videos, and it should. You're paying for somebody who knows what 14 gauge on a 30 amp breaker does, and who's insured when something goes wrong anyway. Your house is the most expensive thing you own and everybody you love sleeps in it.

And if you're ever in your panel and you find a name in Sharpie, call me. I want to know about Ron.
